                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of blurry vision for the past 3 days. He has also had 4 episodes of right-sided headaches over the past month. He has no significant past medical history. His father died of coronary artery disease at the age of 62 years. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 94/min, and blood pressure is 232/128 mm Hg. Fundoscopy shows right-sided optic disc blurring and retinal hemorrhages. A medication is given immediately. Five minutes later, his pulse is 75/min and blood pressure is 190/105 mm Hg. Which of the following drugs was most likely administered?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Labetalol
opb. Hydralazine
opc. Fenoldopam
opd. Nicardipine
ope. Nitroprusside

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with symptoms indicative of a hypertensive emergency, characterized by severely elevated blood pressure (232/128 mm Hg) and signs of end-organ damage (optic disc blurring and retinal hemorrhages). Immediate treatment is necessary to prevent further complications. Labetalol and Nitroprusside are both effective for rapid blood pressure control in emergencies. Labetalol is a common choice due to its dual action as an alpha and beta blocker, providing quick blood pressure reduction. Nitroprusside is also effective but is typically reserved for more severe cases or when immediate control is critical. The observed decrease in pulse and blood pressure after medication administration suggests effective treatment. While Hydralazine, Nicardipine, and Fenoldopam can be used for hypertension, they are not first-line agents for immediate control in hypertensive emergencies. Therefore, the most likely medication administered is Labetalol, supported by its rapid action and common use in such scenarios.
